questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=y{e}^{2x}.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨t,3{t}^{2}⟩$ for $t\in [0,1],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(1,3).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,3)-f(0,0) \\  & =(3{e}^{2\cdot 1})-(0\cdot {e}^{2(0)}) \\  & =3{e}^{2}-0 \\  & =3{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F,$ defined as

$$
F(x,y)=2x{e}^{-y}\,i+(2y-{x}^{2}{e}^{-y})\,j.
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$ for $x\in [2,3].$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

First, we define $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as follows:

$$
F(x,y)={{2x{e}^{-y}}_{⏟}}_{P(x,y)}\,i+{{(2y-{x}^{2}{e}^{-y})}_{⏟}}_{Q(x,y)}\,j.
$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2x{e}^{-y}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2x{e}^{-y}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =2y-{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{-y}+{y}^{2}.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)⟩,\,t\in [2,3].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨2,0⟩, \\ r(3) & =⟨3,\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(2,0)$ and $(3,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(3,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-f(2,0) \\  & =({3}^{2}\cdot {e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2})-({2}^{2}\cdot {e}^{-0}+{0}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}+{ln}^{2}⁡2-4 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+{ln}^{2}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,\pi -1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(\pi ,\pi -1).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(\pi ,\pi -1)-f(0,1) \\  & =(\pi \cdot {e}^{\pi -1}+(\pi -1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0\cdot {e}^{1}+1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(\pi {e}^{\pi -1}+0)-0 \\  & =\pi {e}^{\pi -1}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x,y)={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{y}.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{t}^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩, \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,{\pi }^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(\pi ,{\pi }^{2}).$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=xy^2+ 2xz.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $\mathbf r(t)= \langle e^{t}, t, e^{-t}\rangle$ for $t\in \left[0,1\right],$ evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{C} \nabla f\cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,0,1⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨e,1,\frac{1}{e}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,0,1)$ and $\left(e, 1, \dfrac{1}{e}\right).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e,1,\frac{1}{e})-f(1,0,1) \\  & =(e(1)^{2}+2\cdot e\cdot \frac{1}{e})-(1(0)^{2}+2(1)(1)) \\  & =(e+2)-2 \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y)= xe^{y}.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $x + 2y=3$ for $x\in [-1,1],$ evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{C} \nabla f\cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

We start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t, \dfrac{1}{2}(3-t)\right\rangle, \quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨-1,2⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(-1,2)$ and $(1,1).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(-1)) \\  & =f(1,1)-f(-1,2) \\  & =1\cdot {e}^{1}-(-1)\cdot {e}^{2} \\  & =e+{e}^{2} \\  & =e(1+e).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the curve $C,$ defined parametrically as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t,  1-t \right\rangle, \quad 0 \leq t \leq 1.
$$

Evaluate $\displaystyle{\int _C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r}$ for $\mathbf F = ye^{xy}\,\mathbf i + xe^{xy}\,\mathbf j.$ 

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $\mathbf F$ is conservative.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $\mathbf F = \nabla f.$ Since we're given that $\mathbf F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =y{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =x{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)= e^{xy}.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $\nabla f = \mathbf F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(1,0).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,0)-f(0,1) \\  & ={e}^{1\cdot 0}-{e}^{0\cdot 1} \\  & =1-1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
